Chapter 7 — Orthodontic Treatment Planning
From Problem List to Specific Plan

Treatment Possibilities

I. Dental Crowding: To Expand or Extract? Fig 7.2

Esthetic Consideration

  • When the prominence of the incisors creates excessive lip separation at rest so that the patient must strain to bring the lips together, the teeth are too protrusive and retracting the incisors improves the facial appearance Fig 7.3.
  • You cannot determine the esthetic limit of expansion from tooth‒bone relationships on a cephalometric radiograph.
  • For a patient with a large nose and/or a large chin, moving the incisors forward is better, provided it does not separate the lips too much. For best esthetics, the lower lip should be at least as prominent as the chin Fig 7.4.

Stability Consideration

  • Current guidelines for the limits of expansion of the lower arch Fig 7.5
  • The initial position of the incisors relative to the lip would be a consideration in how much movement could be tolerated.
  • Incisors tipped labially and crowded probably became as protrusive as the facial soft tissues will allow. Moving them any further forward carries great risk of instability.
  • The amount of attached gingiva is a critical variable. If the gingival attachment is questionable, and depending on the amount and direction of planned tooth movement, placing a gingival graft before orthodontic treatment begins may be the best option. (after Periodontist consultation)
  • Expansion across the canines is almost never maintained, especially in the lower arch. In fact, intercanine dimensions typically decrease as patients mature, probably because of lip pressures at the corners of the mouth.
New caution (7th) The 7th edition adds that excessive expansion risks fenestration of the premolar and molar roots through the alveolar bone — with an increasing risk of fenestration beyond 3 mm of transverse tooth movement.

Contemporary Extraction Guidelines for Alignment

  • Contemporary guidelines for orthodontic extraction in Class I crowding cases:
    • Less than 4 mm of arch length discrepancy: Extraction rarely indicated (only if there is severe incisor protrusion or a severe vertical discrepancy). In some cases this amount of crowding can be managed by IPR
    • Arch length discrepancy of 5 to 9 mm: Nonextraction or extraction treatment possible. The decision depends on both the hard and soft tissue characteristics of the patient and on how the final position of the incisors will be.
    • Arch length discrepancy of 10 mm or more: Extraction almost always required. (the amount of crowding virtually equals the amount of tooth mass being removed, and there would be little or no effect on lip support and facial appearance). The extraction choice is four first premolars or perhaps upper first premolars and mandibular lateral incisors (which may provide better long-term stability but requires reshaping of the mandibular canines) Table 7.1.

Dental Protrusion Plus Crowding

  • 2 mm of space in the arch (1 mm on each side) required for 1 mm of retraction of the central incisors.
  • As a general rule, the lips will move about two-thirds of the distance that the incisors are retracted, but there is a great deal of individual variation, primarily because lip retraction stops when the protruding lips come into contact at rest (i.e., when lip competence has been achieved).
  • For that reason, a maximum of 2 to 3 mm of lip retraction is a usual outcome in Class I extraction cases even if the incisors are retracted considerably more than that.
New evidence (7th) Comparable cases treated by extraction or nonextraction differ by only about 2 mm of lip fullness (nonextraction fuller) — the final facial difference is small for most patients. In Black patients, extractions produced more lip retrusion and nonextraction more fullness, so population matters.
  • A final set of guidelines could be as follows:
    • The more you can expand without moving the incisors forward, the more patients you can treat satisfactorily without extraction. (from the perspective of both esthetics and stability)
    • The more you can close extraction spaces without over-retracting the incisors, the more patients you can treat satisfactorily with extraction. (again, from the perspective of both esthetics and stability)
    • For oral health, excessive expansion increase the risk of mucogingival problems.
    • For masticatory function, expansion or extraction makes no difference.

II. Skeletal Problems, Macro-Esthetic Considerations

Orthodontic Camouflage

  • For orthodontic camouflage of mandibular deficiency by retracting the upper incisors tends to be more successful in a northern European‒derived population, in which most people have a convex profile with little or no chin projection.
  • Camouflage of mandibular excess by retracting the lower incisors can be effective in patients of Asian descent, who often have prominence of the lower lip because of protruding incisors than a large mandible.

Surgery

  • Genioplasty, the most frequently used adjunct to orthodontics, also enhances facial appearance by adding volume to the lower face, but in addition it improves the stability of the lower incisors and decreases the chance of gingival stripping by adding bone in front of protruding lower incisors, and so is not just a cosmetic procedure. (functional genioplasty)
  • Orthognathic procedures that decrease volume (mandibular setback and superior repositioning of the maxilla) improve facial proportions but can make the patient look older because of the effects on the skin. For that reason, almost all surgical Class III treatment now includes maxillary advancement, which often is combined with mandibular setback in prognathic patients.

Growth Modification

  • To some extent, jaw growth in all three planes of space can be modified.
  • There is an interesting contrast in success compared with camouflage; greater growth modification is possible in Class III than in Class II patients‒just the reverse of the possibilities for camouflage.

III. Mini-Esthetic Considerations: Improving the Smile Framework

Vertical Tooth‒Lip Relationships

  • In a social smile, the general guideline is that there should be at least 75% display of the central incisor (tooth display is greater in females)
  • The amount of display is a function of the age of the patient, with a peak at adolescence of an average display of 85%, little change up to about age 30, and then a gradual decrease as aging lowers the lips across the anterior teeth.
Updated (7th) The 7th places the display peak before adolescence (still ~85%), with little change up to about the late 20s (your summary, from the 6th, says a peak at adolescence with little change to age 30).
  • There are now three possible treatment approaches to excessive gingival display due to incorrect dental and skeletal relationships: (1) intrusion of the maxillary incisors using segmented arch mechanics, (2) intrusion using temporary skeletal anchorage, and (3) orthognathic surgery to move the maxilla up.
Expanded — gummy smile (7th) The 7th frames the gummy smile around five etiologies — (1) vertical maxillary excess (long-face), (2) short philtrum, (3) short clinical crown height, (4) retroclined maxillary incisors, (5) hypermobile smile — and now lists six treatment options, adding Botox therapy to reduce upper-lip mobility Fig 7.16: with an average gingival-margin-to-lip distance of 5 mm, exposure can be reduced to about 1 mm, lasting ~30–32 weeks (many retreat at 3–4 months).

Transverse Dimensions of the Smile

  • An important consideration in widening a narrow arch form, particularly in an adult, is the axial inclination of the buccal segments. Patients in whom the posterior teeth are already flared laterally are not good candidates for dental expansion.

The Smile Arch

  • Research has suggested that the smile arc is the most important determinant of the attractiveness of the smile‒more important than buccal corridor space, although both play a significant role.
New (7th) The 7th adds that a degree of smile asymmetry can now be addressed — significant cases would need vestibular surgery or Botox (or both) to balance the excessive gingival display (the 6th had regarded smile asymmetry as something that could not be changed).

IV. Micro-Esthetic Considerations: Enhancing the Appearance of the Teeth

Reshaping Teeth

  • Changing Tooth Proportions:
    • The most frequent indication is substituting maxillary canines for congenitally missing maxillary lateral incisors. Closing the space and reshaping the canine to look like a lateral incisor can provide an excellent esthetic result, perhaps superior to an implant in the long run.
  • Correcting Black Triangles:
    • Can be accomplished most readily by removing enamel at the contact point so the teeth can be moved closer together, care is required not to distort the proportional relationships of the teeth to each other.

V. Interaction Between Orthodontist and Restorative Dentist

  • There are two ways to manage the orthodontic-restorative interaction:
    1. Carefully plan where the teeth are to be placed, place a vacuum-formed retainer immediately after the orthodontic appliance is removed (full time), and send the patient to the restorative dentist for completion of the treatment. A new retainer is needed as soon as the restorations have been completed.
    2. An alternative, which is most applicable when composite build-ups rather than laminates are planned. Remove the brackets from the teeth to be restored, send the patient immediately to the restorative dentist, replace the brackets the same day after the restorations are completed, and close any residual space before removing the orthodontic appliance.

VI. Reshaping Gingival Contours: Applications of a Soft Tissue Laser

  • Treatment of this type now can be carried out effectively with the use of a diode laser.
  • A laser of this type has two primary advantages: (1) It does not cut hard tissue, and (2) it creates a "biologic dressing" because it coagulates, sterilizes, and seals the soft tissue as it is used.
Treatment Planning in Special Circumstances

I. Dental Disease Problems

  • Endodontically treated teeth respond to orthodontic force in the same way as teeth with vital pulps.
  • In general, prior endodontic treatment does not contraindicate orthodontic tooth movement, but teeth with a history of severe trauma may be at greater risk of root resorption, whether they have received endodontic treatment or not.
  • Children or adults with a lack of adequate attached gingiva in the mandibular anterior region should have free gingival grafts to create attached gingiva before the beginning of orthodontics.

II. Systemic Disease Problems

  • Patients with systemic disease are at greater risk for complications during orthodontic treatment but can have successful orthodontic treatment as long as the systemic problems are under control.

Diabetes

  • In adults or children, the most common systemic problem that may complicate orthodontic treatment
  • If the diabetes is under good control, periodontal responses to orthodontic force are essentially normal.
  • The rapid progression of alveolar bone loss in patients with diabetes is well recognized, however, and if diabetes is not under good control, there is a real risk of accelerated periodontal breakdown Fig 7.29.
  • Careful monitoring of a diabetic patient's compliance with medical therapy is essential during orthodontic treatment. Prolonged comprehensive orthodontic treatment should be avoided in these patients.

Rheumatoid Arthritis

  • Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA) can produce severe skeletal mandibular deficiency, and adult-onset rheumatoid arthritis can destroy the condylar process and create a deformity Fig 7.30.
  • Reduced mandibular growth has been reported after steroid injections into the temporomandibular joint in JRA treatment, and long-term administration of steroids as part of the medical treatment may increase the possibility of periodontal problems during orthodontics.
  • Children on steroids may also be taking bisphosphonates, which make orthodontic tooth movement almost impossible. Prolonged orthodontic treatment should be avoided in patients with either type of rheumatoid arthritis because the potential for harm is at least as great as the potential benefit.

Pregnancy

  • Gingival hyperplasia is likely to be a problem, Hormonal variations in pregnancy sometimes can lead to surprising results from otherwise predictable treatment procedures.
  • Because of bone turnover issues during pregnancy and lactation, an orthodontist theoretically should be vigilant about loss of alveolar bone and root resorption during pregnancy, but radiographs to check on the status of bone and tooth roots are not permissible then. Treatment for a potential patient who is already pregnant should be deferred until the pregnancy is completed.
  • If a patient becomes pregnant during treatment, the possible problems should be discussed, and it is wise to place her in a holding pattern during the last trimester, limiting the amount of active tooth movement.

III. Jaw Injuries

  • If the maxilla is displaced by trauma, it should be repositioned immediately if this is possible.
  • When immediate attention to a displaced maxilla is impossible because of other injuries, protraction force from a facemask before fractures have completely healed can successfully reposition it.
  • Mandibular asymmetry with deficient growth but some translation on that side is a particular indication for custom-designed "hybrid" functional appliances. (in growing patients)
  • The severe restriction of growth that accompanies little or no translation of the condyle can lead to a progressively more severe deformity. Progressive deformity of this type is an indication for early surgical intervention and orthodontic treatment with a hybrid functional appliance usually is needed after surgery to release ankylosis to guide the subsequent growth.

IV. Hemimandibular Hypertrophy

  • Mandibular and facial asymmetry can also be caused by excessive growth of a mandibular condyle or lengthening of the condylar neck. Growth problems of this type are never symmetric.
  • It is simply excessive growth on one side of normal condylar tissue, with no histologic difference from normal condyles.
  • There are two possible modes of treatment, both surgical:
    • Ramus osteotomy (after the excessive growth has ceased)
    • Condylectomy to remove the excessively growing condyle and reconstruct the joint.
  • Removal of the condyle is likely to be necessary in the more severe and more rapidly growing cases, whereas a ramus osteotomy is preferred for the less severe problems (after growth is ceased).
  • The bone-seeking isotope technetium 99m (Tc) can be used to distinguish an active rapidly growing condyle from an enlarged condyle that has ceased growing Fig 7.31. Unfortunately, although false-positive images are rare, false-negative images are not, so a negative bone scan of the condyles cannot be taken as evidence that hyperplastic growth of one condyle is not occurring.

V. Sleep Apnea

  • The pharyngeal airway can be seen on lateral cephalometric radiographs Fig 7.32. But the depth of the airway is not shown in cephalograms, and therefore the location of the minimum dimension of the airway cannot be located.
  • Even with three-dimensional images, one gets only a snapshot of the airway, which undergoes small changes minute to minute and larger changes between upright and supine body positions and between being awake and being asleep.
  • Mandibular deficiency is by no means the major risk factor for sleep apnea. Obesity (fat deposits in the neck) and increasing age (Muscle tone decrease) are major contributing factors.
  • Intra-oral appliances can be effective for some patients with low or moderately severe sleep apnea. It should be designed to minimize tooth movement, which can occur easily if the appliance puts prolonged pressure on the teeth during sleep.
  • Orthognathic surgery to advance the mandible and maxilla to provide more room for the tongue is important in treating severely affected patients.
  • Opening the midpalatal suture orthodontically does help some children with sleep apnea. Surgical maxillary expansion in adults with sleep apnea both opens the nasal passage and widens the upper pharyngeal area.
New — sleep-apnea detail (7th) The 7th greatly expands this section:
  • Children: the first-line treatment remains adenotonsillectomy (oral appliances/expansion are alternatives when adenotonsillar tissue isn't the cause or symptoms persist after surgery).
  • Adults: oral appliances completely resolve OSA in only 29% to 71% of patients (~⅓ get no benefit); maxillomandibular advancement (MMA) surgery gave a >50% AHI reduction in 85% of 518 patients (full cure <40%); and a new option — hypoglossal nerve stimulation (genioglossus protrusion) — is introduced.

VI. Cleft Lip and Palate

  • Orthodontic treatment may be involved at any or all of four separate stages: Table 7.2
    1. In infancy before the initial surgical repair of the lip
    2. During the late primary and early mixed dentition
    3. During the late mixed and early permanent dentition
    4. In the late teens after the completion of facial growth, in conjunction with orthognathic surgery.

Infant Orthopedics

  • In patients with a bilateral cleft, the premaxillary segment is often displaced anteriorly while the posterior maxillary segments are lingually collapsed behind it Fig 7.34. Less severe distortions occur in infants with unilateral palatal clefts Fig 7.35A‒B.
  • Orthodontic intervention to reposition the segments and to bring the protruding premaxillary segment back into the arch may be needed to obtain a good surgical repair of the lip.
  • In a child with a bilateral cleft, two types of movement of the maxillary segments may be needed. First, the collapsed maxillary posterior segments must be expanded laterally; then pressure against the premaxilla can reposition it posteriorly into its approximately correct position in the arch. This can be accomplished by:
    • A light elastic strap across the anterior segment
    • An orthodontic appliance pinned to the segments that applies a contraction force
    • Or even by pressure from the repaired lip if lip repair is done after the lateral expansion.
  • If presurgical movement of maxillary segments is indicated, this typically would be done beginning at 3 to 6 weeks of age so that the lip closure can be carried out at approximately 10 weeks. A passive plate, similar to an orthodontic retainer, is then used for a few months after lip closure Fig 7.35C‒D.
  • Alveolar bone grafts are better deferred until the early mixed dentition.
New technique (7th) The 7th introduces nasoalveolar molding (NAM) as an option for presurgical infant orthopedics — a NAM plate moves the maxillary segments and shapes the nose, while lip taping (and lip adhesion surgery) helps retract the premaxilla and narrow the cleft before final lip repair.

Late Primary and Early Mixed Dentition Treatment

  • Many of the orthodontic problems of children with cleft palate in the late and early mixed dentition result not from the cleft itself but from the effects of surgical repair.
  • Closure of the lip inevitably creates some constriction across the anterior part of the maxillary arch, and closure of a cleft palate causes at least some degree of lateral constriction.
  • As a result, surgically treated cleft palate patients have a tendency toward both anterior and lateral crossbite, which is not seen in patients with untreated clefts.
  • As the permanent teeth come in, there is a strong tendency for the maxillary incisors to erupt rotated and often in crossbite. The major goal of orthodontic treatment (in this stage) is to correct incisor position and prepare the patient for an alveolar bone graft.
  • The objective is to have a permanent tooth erupt through the grafted area so that the cleft is obliterated.
    • If the permanent lateral incisors are present, the graft should be placed at about age 7, before they erupt.
    • If the laterals are missing, the graft can be delayed but should be done before the permanent canines erupt.
  • Any necessary alignment of incisors or expansion of posterior segments should be completed before the alveolar grafting. For bilateral cleft patients, an expander (fan expander) that expands more anteriorly than posteriorly has been shown to be more effective.

Early Permanent Dentition Treatment

  • As the canine and premolar teeth erupt, posterior crossbite is likely to develop.
  • New bone fills in the grafted cleft as the canine erupts, which makes it possible to close spaces due to missing teeth, and this now is a major objective of this phase of treatment "comprehensive orthodontic treatment." Fig 7.36
  • If space closure is not possible, orthodontic tooth movement may be needed to position teeth as abutments for eventual fixed prosthodontics. In that circumstance, a resin-bonded bridge.

Orthognathic Surgery for Patients With Cleft Lip and Palate

  • Continued mandibular growth after the completion of active orthodontic treatment leads to the return of anterior and lateral crossbites.
  • This result is not so much from excessive mandibular growth as from deficient maxillary growth, both anteroposteriorly and vertically.
  • Orthognathic surgery to bring the deficient maxilla downward and forward may be a necessary last stage in treatment of a patient with cleft lip or palate, typically at about age 18 if required.
New subsections (7th) Beyond clefting, the 7th adds dedicated craniofacial-anomaly subsections: Hemifacial Microsomia (HFM) — asymmetric deficiency of the ear, ramus and soft tissues — and Craniosynostosis (premature cranial-suture fusion), which occurs in about 1 in 2000 to 2500 live births.
